title: Latency from raw log lines
prompt: Many log records carry the request's latency in `attributes.latency_ms`, as text. Write `solve(application_logs_raw)` with RDD functions so it returns `log_id`, `service` and `latency_ms` (a whole number) for every record whose latency is usable.
rules: Only lines that are JSON objects count; skip broken lines, plain text and JSON that isn't an object.
A latency is usable only when `attributes.latency_ms` is text made only of the digits 0–9, such as `"42"` or `"0"`. Skip `"12.5"`, `"-5"`, `"fast"` and empty text.
Skip records with no `attributes`, a null one, one that isn't an object, or no `latency_ms` key. A record without `log_id` or `service` gives NULL there.
Keep repeated records. Return `log_id`, `service` (text) and `latency_ms` (`int`), in that order.
hints: Parse each line safely with a function that returns `[record]` or `[]`, and use `flatMap`.
A second `flatMap` can decide per record: return `[(log_id, service, ms)]` to keep it or `[]` to drop it.
Check every step: is `attributes` a dict, is the value a `str`, and does `value.isdigit()` hold? Only then call `int(value)`.
explanation: Two `flatMap` steps keep this safe: `parse` turns each line into `[record]` or `[]`, and a second function returns `[(log_id, service, int(value))]` only when `attributes` is a dict and its `latency_ms` is a string for which `isdigit()` is true. `int(value)` inside a `try` isn't the same rule: it accepts `"-5"`. Calling `.get` on a null or list `attributes` stops the whole job, and a schema string with `latency_ms int` gives the whole-number column.
